meta.title_plain: How online games send your move to the server and back
meta.teaser: Packets, servers and ping: why your game sometimes lags.

page.title: How online games send your move to the server and back
page.sub: The science behind online gaming lag
page.bigIdea: Every move you make is chopped into tiny packets that race to a game server and back. The faster that round trip, the less lag you feel.

cards.title: Your move becomes packets
cards.front: You tap jump. What actually leaves your phone?
cards.back: Your move becomes small chunks of data called packets. Each has a header with the address, like an envelope, and a payload, the message inside.
cards.tryit: Write a sentence across 4 numbered sticky notes. Shuffle them and ask someone to rebuild it using the numbers.

cards.title: Routers pass it along
cards.front: Your packet doesn't fly straight to the game.
cards.back: Routers read each packet's address and pass it on, one hop at a time. Each hop adds a tiny delay, like a ball passed down a line.
cards.tryit: Pass a tennis ball through 3 people and time it. Then try 6 people. Which was faster?

cards.title: The server is the referee
cards.front: Who decides if your shot really hit?
cards.back: Online games keep the real game on a central server. Your device asks to move. The server decides and tells every player, like an umpire calling in or out.
cards.tryit: In your next match, notice a moment when the game seems to 'take back' something you did.

cards.title: Ping is the round trip
cards.front: That little number in the corner means a lot.
cards.back: Ping is how long a message takes to reach the server and come back, in milliseconds. Over 100 ms usually feels laggy. Far-away servers mean longer trips.
cards.tryit: Look in a game's settings for a ping or network stats option. Watch how the number changes.

cards.title: Games guess to hide lag
cards.back: While waiting for the server, your game predicts where players are heading. When a guess is wrong, a player snaps back or 'warps'. That's prediction fixing itself.
cards.tryit: Roll a ball, close your eyes and point where it will be in 2 seconds. Open them. How close were you?

words.d: A small chunk of data with an address, sent across a network.
A device that reads packet addresses and sends them the right way.
A powerful computer that runs the real game for all players.
The time for a message to reach the server and return.
The delay between your action and the game showing its result.

quiz.q: What does a packet's header hold?
quiz.hint: Think about what's written on the outside of an envelope.
quiz.why: The header holds addresses so routers know where to send the packet.

quiz.q: Which ping would feel smoothest in a match?
quiz.hint: Is ping a score to beat, or a time you have to wait?
quiz.why: Ping is waiting time, so a smaller number means a faster round trip.

quiz.q: Why do online games use a central server?
opts: So one place decides what really happened
quiz.hint: Think about why a tennis match needs an umpire.
quiz.why: One server keeps the true game so every player sees the same result.

quiz.q: Why can a far-away server cause more lag?
opts: Packets travel farther through more hops
quiz.hint: Remember the ball passed through 3 people versus 6.
quiz.why: A longer trip with more routers adds delay each way.

page.think: If you built an online game for players all over the world, where would you put your servers, and why?
